title: Flexible pavement layers and the fourth power law of axle damage

explain.say: From 1958 to 1960, near Ottawa in Illinois, army drivers drove loaded trucks round test loops day and night until the roads broke. This was the AASHO Road Test, and it still shapes how roads are designed. On the board is a flexible pavement, the kind with an asphalt top, cut open layer by layer.

explain.say: A loaded wheel presses on a small patch, about the size of a dinner plate, at about five hundred and sixty kilopascals. Each layer spreads the load wider, like a pyramid of acrobats. By the top of the soil, about fifty five centimetres down, the pressure is only about thirty kilopascals, roughly one eighteenth. Which layer does most of that spreading?

explain.say: The thick stone base! Now look at the bottom, the subgrade, the natural soil. Its strength is measured by CBR, the California bearing ratio, a percentage of the strength of a standard crushed rock. Soft clay might be three percent, good gravel thirty. The weaker the soil, the thicker the layers on top must be.

layers.label: Base course
layers.ask: How does a flexible pavement spread the wheel load?

explain.say: Here is the big lesson of the road test. Damage grows with the fourth power of axle load. A standard axle of eighty kilonewtons counts as one. A hundred kilonewton axle does two point four times the damage, and a doubled axle of a hundred and sixty does sixteen times. Which do you think harms roads most: cars, or overloaded trucks?

curves.label: Fourth power law
curves.ask: What is the fourth power law?

explain.say: Overloaded trucks, by far! An eight kilonewton car axle does one ten thousandth of a standard axle's damage. So engineers design roads for the number of standard axles expected, often millions. Excellent work! Challenge: how many times more damage does a hundred and twenty kilonewton axle do than a standard one?

faq.q: What are the layers of a flexible pavement?
faq.a: From the top: a bituminous surface course, a binder course, a granular base, a granular sub-base and the compacted subgrade soil. Each layer is stronger than the one below it.

faq.q: How does a flexible pavement spread the wheel load?
faq.a: Each layer spreads the load over a wider area, so the pressure falls with depth. A 560 kilopascal tyre pressure drops to about 30 kilopascals at 0.55 metres depth.
The California bearing ratio compares the load needed to push a plunger into a soil with the load for a standard crushed rock, as a percentage. Low CBR soils need thicker pavements.
asks: How does CBR affect pavement thickness?

faq.q: What is the fourth power law?
faq.a: From the AASHO Road Test: pavement damage grows roughly with the fourth power of axle load. An axle twice as heavy does about 16 times the damage.
A single axle with dual wheels carrying 80 kilonewtons, about 8.2 tonnes. Mixed traffic is converted into equivalent standard axles for design.

facts: The AASHO Road Test ran near Ottawa, Illinois, from 1958 to 1960.
Pavement design converts mixed traffic into equivalent standard axles of 80 kN (18,000 lb).
